meta.name: Can Dogs Eat Yogurt? Yes — Plain Unsweetened, in Small Amounts
meta.title_tag: Can Dogs Eat Yogurt? Yes, Plain & Small
meta.excerpt: Plain unsweetened yogurt is safe for most dogs and a popular source of probiotics. Avoid flavored yogurts entirely — many contain xylitol, which is fatal to dogs even in small doses. Stick to plain whole-milk or low-fat yogurt with no artificial sweeteners.
meta.meta_description: Plain yogurt is safe and beneficial for dogs in small amounts. Learn which yogurts to choose, which to avoid (xylitol warning), and how much to feed.

hero.alt: A bowl of plain Greek yogurt with a wooden spoon on a kitchen counter beside a small ceramic dog bowl — plain unsweetened yogurt is safe for dogs

body_html:
Quick Answer: Yes — plain unsweetened yogurt is safe for most dogs in small amounts and is a popular natural source of probiotics. The critical exception is flavored or low-sugar yogurts: many contain xylitol, an artificial sweetener that is fatal to dogs even in tiny amounts. Always read the label and only feed plain, unsweetened yogurt with no artificial sweeteners.

The Short Answer: Yes, Plain Yogurt Only

Plain unsweetened yogurt is one of the most popular dairy products recommended for dogs by veterinarians and dog nutritionists. It is rich in protein, calcium, and live probiotic cultures, and it is well-tolerated by most adult dogs in small amounts. The key word is plain. Flavored, low-fat, low-sugar, and "diet" yogurts frequently contain artificial sweeteners, and one of those sweeteners — xylitol — is acutely toxic to dogs and can be fatal in doses as small as a few grams.

Treated correctly, yogurt is a useful treat and a common ingredient in homemade dog food and frozen treat recipes. Treated carelessly, the wrong yogurt becomes one of the most dangerous things in a refrigerator.

Why Yogurt Is Beneficial for Dogs

The health benefits of plain yogurt come from three components:

  • Probiotic bacteria. Yogurts made with live cultures (look for "live and active cultures" on the label) contain Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species that support gut health, particularly after antibiotic use or during digestive upset.
  • Protein and calcium. A typical serving of plain yogurt delivers high-quality protein, calcium, phosphorus, and B vitamins. Greek yogurt is more protein-dense than regular yogurt.
  • Lower lactose than milk. The fermentation process consumes much of the lactose in milk, making yogurt more digestible than milk for most lactose-sensitive adult dogs.

Yogurt is sometimes recommended as a natural support after diarrhea or antibiotic treatment, although veterinarians increasingly prefer dog-specific probiotic supplements with strains and CFU counts validated for canine gut health.

The Xylitol Danger: Why Flavored Yogurts Are Off-Limits

Xylitol is a sugar alcohol increasingly used as an artificial sweetener in low-sugar yogurts, peanut butters, gums, mints, and baked goods. In humans, it is metabolized slowly and contributes few calories. In dogs, xylitol triggers a rapid release of insulin, producing severe hypoglycemia within 10–60 minutes. Higher doses cause acute liver failure within 12–72 hours.

Yogurts marketed as low-sugar, light, sugar-free, or carb-conscious frequently contain xylitol without obvious warning on the front of the package. Always check the ingredient list. Look for "xylitol", "wood sugar", "birch sugar", or any sugar alcohol other than erythritol.

If a dog has eaten any yogurt with xylitol, this is a medical emergency. Call your veterinarian or the ASPCA Poison Control line (888-426-4435) immediately, even if no symptoms have appeared.

What Yogurt to Choose for Dogs

Safe options:

  • Plain whole-milk Greek yogurt — highest protein, lower lactose due to straining. The most popular choice.
  • Plain regular (whole-milk) yogurt — standard option, fine for most dogs.
  • Plain low-fat or non-fat yogurt — acceptable, though some brands compensate with added thickeners or stabilizers.
  • Goat-milk yogurt (unsweetened) — popular in raw-feeding communities; very low lactose.

Avoid: flavored, fruit-on-the-bottom, vanilla, low-sugar, sugar-free, or "natural sweetened" yogurts. Avoid coconut-milk yogurts only if they contain xylitol or chocolate flavoring.

Serving Size and Frequency

Yogurt is rich, so portions should be modest:

  • Small dog (under 20 lb): 1 to 2 teaspoons.
  • Medium dog (20–50 lb): 1 to 2 tablespoons.
  • Large dog (50+ lb): 2 to 4 tablespoons.

Two to three servings per week is plenty for most dogs. Yogurt is often used as a spoon-licked food topper, a Kong filler before freezing, or mixed into a bland diet of plain rice and chicken during digestive recovery.

When to Avoid Yogurt

  • Lactose intolerance. If a dog gets diarrhea after yogurt, even plain yogurt is too much dairy. Switch to a dog-specific probiotic.
  • Pancreatitis history. Choose non-fat yogurt and feed only in tiny amounts, or skip altogether.
  • Significant overweight. The calorie load adds up; use a lower-calorie reward.
  • Any yogurt of unknown ingredients. If you cannot read the label, do not feed it.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Greek yogurt better for dogs?

Yes for most dogs. Greek yogurt is strained, which removes much of the whey and concentrates protein while reducing lactose. Plain whole-milk Greek yogurt is the most commonly recommended choice for dogs.

Can I give my dog yogurt every day?

You can, but most dogs do not need it daily. The probiotics in yogurt are useful but a small portion two or three times per week delivers most of the benefit without contributing excess calories.

What if my dog ate yogurt with xylitol?

This is a true emergency. Call your veterinarian or ASPCA Poison Control (888-426-4435) immediately, even if your dog seems fine. Hypoglycemia can develop within 10–60 minutes; liver failure can develop hours later. Bring the container with the ingredient list.

Is frozen yogurt safe for dogs?

Plain yogurt frozen at home is safe. Store-bought "frozen yogurt" is usually a sweetened dessert and frequently contains xylitol or chocolate; treat it as unsafe unless you can verify the ingredients.

Is yogurt the same as kefir for dogs?

Kefir is a thinner fermented dairy beverage with a broader spectrum of probiotic strains than yogurt. Both are reasonable, plain and unsweetened. Kefir is increasingly popular in raw-feeding communities for digestive support.
